comments.author: @immmersive
comments.text:
This is just hype which feeds into growing the AI bubble. A lot of businesses are banking on AI, but once the time comes and nothing is delivered the bubble will burst.  Their classification is all wrong, because they are using problem-solving performance to assess the degree of AGI levels. This is fine for the narrow AI, but not for general AI.  Think about it folks, a 5yo child has general intelligence, but is way below in problem-solving skills than an average grownup. General intelligence has nothing to do with how good you are at solving problems, but how well you can generalize.

We are currently at Level 0 AGI and will stay there for a while, so let’s try to understand why:

1. What should AGI be defined as?

The idea behind general problem-solving is to show that you can generalize patterns, at least to some degree. What we need at a base level to get to AGI, is for the machine to be able to recognize patterns, derive rules from the patterns and use those rules to solve a similar case when presented with problems they have not been trained on. AI currently fails at that, if you present it with a simple example, such as the ARC-AGI test. Thus, failing at the first step of being called AGI.  

2. So, where's the problem in reaching AGI?

The problem is that current AI algorithms lack the ability to generalize and create abstraction across different classes of problems. AI needs this ability, because you need to use patterns, to create a simplified model from observable cases presented. This is what generalization is. Deriving rules from examples is generalization and we need to be able to generalize in order to create abstractions. These are simpler models of reality, which still maintain certain level of information, with respect to which, we are creating the abstract model. 

An example would be a human being. Let's say you observe many human beings and someone asks you to create a model of a person to add to a database. If this task is for a hotel booking website, you will take important traits, which most people have, like 

- name
- address 
- phone number

On the other hand, if its for medical purposes and you want to understand some biological relation on large populations, you will probably take into account traits like:

- height
- weight
- age
- eye color

You would then have 2 different systems to classify people. Each system excels at a different task, because it presents an abstraction which presents different information. Depending on what we want to do with this info, we would pick the correct system for solving our task. Either a booking website, or medical analysis.

3. So how would general problem-solving work in real world?

Simple, you would be presented with one type of problem, be trained on it and solve many cases. Then, you would be presented with a different type of problem and either be instantly able to solve it or figure out how to do it. In either case, you would do that from generalized knowledge from your first problem. The idea would be to recognize patterns which helped you to solve the first type of problem and derive similar solution to the second-type of problem  The trick is to be able to create the correct abstraction model by understanding how to generalize correctly. That is, which traits are needed, with respect to goal we are trying to accomplish.

In the real world, humans do this all the time. AI on the other hand fails miserably. AI trained on image recognition, will know nothing about voice generation and vice versa. AI currently is only trained on one particular type of problems, and it can only solve those type of problems when tasked to do so. It can't solve different types of problems, either instantly, or by learning it by itself.
